name: Example: Finding the Maclaurin Expansion of a Logarithmic Function
problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the expansion of $f(x) = \ln{\left(\dfrac{1+2x}{1+x}\right)}.$
worked_solution:
First, using the laws of logarithms, we observe that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+2x}{1+x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+2x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the expansion of $\ln(1+x),$ we use the standard result

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) & =x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

To obtain the expansion of $\ln{(1+2x)},$ we replace $x$ with $2x$ in the standard expansion:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+2x) & =2x-\frac{1}{2}(2x)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(2x)^{3}-⋯ \\  & =2x-2{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we subtract the two series to give the desired result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+2x}{1+x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+2x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) \\  & =(2x-2{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯)-(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯) \\  & =x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{7}{3}{x}^{3}-⋯\end{aligned}
$$

For the series $\ln(1+2x),$ the radius of convergence is given by

$$
-1 < 2x \leq 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in \left(-\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right].
$$

The series $\ln(1+x)$ has a radius of convergence of $x\in(-1,1].$ Therefore, the radius of convergence of $f(x)$ is

$$
x\in \left(-\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right] \cap (-1,1] = \left(-\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right] .
$$
